People prosper while they hasten to break the fast, as the Prophet did, breaking it once the sun sets and night comes from the east, even on a journey.
The Prophet forbade uninterrupted fasting, being unlike them as his Lord fed him and gave him drink, and said he would have prolonged it to deter those who persisted.
Aisha reported that the Prophet kissed and embraced his wives while fasting, adding that none controlled his desire as he did.
Aisha, Hafsa and Umm Salama reported the Prophet kissing while fasting; when the questioner said Allah had forgiven his sins, he replied he was the most God-conscious of them.
Aisha and Umm Salama said the Prophet sometimes woke junub from intercourse at dawn and still fasted, and Abu Huraira withdrew his contrary view, which he had from Fadl.
A man who had intercourse by day in Ramadan was told to free a slave, fast two months or feed sixty poor; having nothing, he received food for his family.
In Ramadan of the year of Victory the Prophet set out for Mecca fasting, then drank publicly and broke the fast, calling those who kept fasting disobedient.
Seeing a crowd shading a man who was fasting on a journey, the Prophet said it is no righteousness to fast on a journey, and to take Allah's concession.
Travelling in Ramadan, some companions fasted and some did not, without blame; those not fasting did the work and took the reward, and facing the enemy all broke it.
Hamza al-Aslami was told he may fast on a journey or not, the concession being from Allah, and on a hot journey only the Prophet and Abdullah b. Rawaha fasted.
When people disputed whether the Prophet was fasting on the day of Arafa, Umm al-Fadl, or Maimuna, sent him a cup of milk and he drank it at Arafa.
Quraysh fasted Ashura before Islam and the Prophet commanded it, but once fasting Ramadan became obligatory, he left Ashura optional, calling it one of the days of Allah.
Ibn Mas'ud ate on Ashura, its fast having been left once Ramadan became obligatory, and Mu'awiya quoted the Prophet: Allah did not make it obligatory, though he himself was fasting.
Finding the Jews fasting Ashura for Moses' deliverance from Pharaoh, and treating it as a festival, the Prophet said Muslims are closer to Moses and ordered it fasted.
Ibn Abbas taught fasting the ninth of Muharram; told Jews and Christians revere Ashura, the Prophet said he would fast the ninth next year, but died first.
On Ashura the Prophet had it announced that even those who had eaten should fast the rest of the day, and fasting children were given woollen toys.
The Prophet forbade fasting on the two days of Eid, Fitr and Adha; Ibn Umar, asked about a vow falling on one, cited this ban beside the duty of vows.
The days of Tashriq, the days of Mina, are days of eating, drinking and remembering Allah, and it was announced then that none but a believer enters Paradise.
The Prophet forbade singling out Friday for fasting unless joined to the day before and after or a habitual fast, and singling out its night for prayer.
The verse letting those able to fast feed a needy person instead was abrogated by the verse that whoever witnesses the month must fast it.
Aisha could make up the Ramadan fasts she missed only in Sha'ban, because of her duties to the Prophet.
The heir fasts what a dead person owed, Allah's debt being most deserving of payment, and a woman was told to fast and perform Hajj for her dead mother.
One fasting replies 'I am fasting' to invitations or insults; Allah Himself rewards fasting, a shield, prizing the faster's breath above musk, and Paradise's gate Rayyan admits only fasters.
Whoever fasts a day in the way of Allah, Allah removes his face seventy years' distance from Hell.
Finding no food the Prophet would fast, yet ate a gift of hais though he had fasted since morning, and one who eats forgetfully while fasting should complete the fast.
Apart from Ramadan the Prophet never fasted a whole month, at times fasting or not fasting so long people thought he would never change, and fasted most in Sha'ban.
Abdullah b. Amr, fasting daily and praying all night, was told to fast three days monthly or at most David's alternate days, the best fast, and recite the Quran weekly.
Three days monthly with Ramadan is perpetual fasting, alternate days are David's fast, Arafa and Ashura fasts expiate sins, and a missed mid-month fast is made up with two days.
The best fast after Ramadan is in Allah's month al-Muharram, the best prayer after the obligatory is at night, and Ramadan with six Shawwal fasts is like perpetual fasting.
Seeing companions' dreams agree, the Prophet said to seek Lailat-ul-Qadr in the last seven or ten nights of Ramadan, the odd ones, and said he was shown it but forgot.
Seeking Lailat-ul-Qadr in i'tikaf, the Prophet was told it lay in the last ten odd nights and saw himself prostrating in water and clay, which rain left on his forehead.
Seek Lailat-ul-Qadr in the last ten nights; Ubayy b. Ka'b swore it is the twenty-seventh, with a rayless sunrise, and the Prophet mentioned a moon like a piece of plate.
The Prophet kept i'tikaf in Ramadan's last ten days until his death, his wives after him, and once, seeing his wives' tents, struck his own and moved it to Shawwal.
In the last ten nights the Prophet stayed awake, woke his family and exerted himself in devotion more than at any other time.
Aisha never saw the Prophet fasting in the ten days of Dhu'l-Hijja.
One in ihram may not wear a shirt, turban, trousers, cap or saffron-dyed cloth, but one without a lower garment or shoes may wear trousers or trimmed socks.
At Ji'rana, after revelation came upon him, the Prophet told a man in ihram for Umrah to wash off his perfume, remove his cloak and do as in Hajj.
The Prophet fixed where to enter ihram: Dhu'l-Hulaifa for Medina, Juhfa for Syria, Qarn al-Manazil for Najd, Yalamlam for Yemen, Mecca for Meccans; Jabir's report adds Dhat al-'Irq for Iraq.
The Prophet's Talbiya, 'Here I am at Thy service', affirms Allah has no partner and owns praise, grace and sovereignty; Umar and Ibn Umar added words, polytheists added a partner.
The Prophet, after a night and prayer at Dhu'l-Hulaifa, began Talbiya as his camel stood up by its mosque, not at al-Baida', and Ibn Umar modelled four habits on him.
